```

## What changes along a regularization path?

This tutorial follows the Lasso [@tibshirani_regression_1996a], Adaptive
Lasso [@zou.2006], Group Lasso [@yuan_lin.2006] and Adaptive Group Lasso
[@wangleng2008csda]. General background on regularization paths and
model selection is given by @hastie_etal.2015.

Increasing the penalty changes the estimated coefficients, the selected variables
and the sensitivity of the fit to the data. These are related, but different,
quantities. This tutorial follows all three on a common grid, first for Lasso
and Adaptive Lasso, then for Group Lasso and Adaptive Group Lasso.

We use simulated data so that the true coefficients and the conditional mean
are known. The aim is to understand the methods and their outputs, not to
establish a performance ranking from one realization. We will:

1. construct a reproducible regression problem;
2. inspect coefficient paths and selected slices of those paths;
3. compare divergence with counts of selected coordinates and groups;
4. separate the fixed-weight contribution from the adaptive correction;
5. relate tuning choices to independent test performance;
6. check one analytic divergence against numerical differentiation.

### Packages and graphical conventions

```{r libraries}
library(spares)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

All path plots use a logarithmic horizontal axis labelled $\lambda$.
Moving **right** means a stronger penalty. Lines join computed grid points;
they do not imply continuity at changes of the active set. Estimates returned
by `coef(fit, s=...)` between knots use interpolation rather than an exact refit.

The objective uses $\mathrm{RSS}/(2n)$, so the parameter $\gamma$ in a formulation
using $\mathrm{RSS}/2$ is $\gamma=n\lambda$. A common numerical $\lambda$ does
not represent identical regularization across different penalties or weights.

## Generate data with a known structure

There are twelve correlated predictors in four disjoint groups of size three.
Only the first two groups contain signal; the second contains both nonzero and
zero coefficients. This illustrates the distinction between selecting a group
and selecting every coordinate individually.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100
p <- 12
groups <- rep(1:4, each = 3)
Sigma <- outer(seq_len(p), seq_len(p), function(i, j) 0.35^abs(i-j))
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), n, p) %*% chol(Sigma)
colnames(X) <- paste0('x', seq_len(p))
beta_true <- c(1.5, -1, 0.8, 1, -0.7, 0, rep(0, 6))
intercept_true <- 1
sigma <- 0.8
mu <- as.numeric(intercept_true + X %*% beta_true)
y <- mu + rnorm(n, sd = sigma)
knitr::kable(data.frame(variable=colnames(X), group=groups,
                       coefficient=beta_true), digits=2)
```

Predictors have the same population variance. We do not standardize them in
this example: the design matrix is held fixed throughout fitting and the
numerical derivative check. An unpenalized intercept is included in every fit.
The OLS pilot is identifiable because the full design has full column rank
and $n>p+1$.

### A common positive grid

```{r grid}
lambda <- 10^seq(1, -2.5, length.out = 60)
control <- list(maxit=20000, abstol=1e-10, reltol=1e-10, print.out=FALSE)
```

This geometric grid spans strong to weak regularization. It is specified
before looking at the response and reused for all methods. The upper end
should produce an intercept-only fit; we check this rather than assuming it.
For routine analyses, automatic grids and `lambdamax()` are also available.

## Lasso and Adaptive Lasso

The Lasso uses fixed coordinate weights. Adaptive Lasso uses the full-design
OLS pilot with exponential weights $\omega_j(r)=e^{-r}$. Large pilot magnitudes
receive smaller penalties. This finite profile also avoids a singular weight
at a zero pilot; inverse-power weights are covered in the workflow vignette.

```{r scalar-fits}
fit_lasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='lasso', intercept=TRUE,
                   standardize=FALSE, lambda=lambda, control=control)
fit_adalasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='adalasso', profile='exponential',
                      exponent=1, intercept=TRUE, standardize=FALSE,
                      lambda=lambda, control=control)
fits <- list('Lasso'=fit_lasso, 'Adaptive Lasso'=fit_adalasso)
```

### Extract estimates and check diagnostics

`beta` has one row per penalized variable and one column per regularization
value. `a0` stores the intercept path; `coef()` includes it in coefficient
extraction. `dof()` returns one row per regularization value, including the
status of the derivative calculation.

```{r helpers}
path_data <- function(fit, method) {
  data.frame(method=method, lambda=rep(fit$lambda, each=nrow(fit$beta)),
             variable=factor(rep(colnames(X), times=length(fit$lambda)), levels=colnames(X)),
             estimate=as.vector(fit$beta),
             group=factor(rep(groups, times=length(fit$lambda))))
}
coefficient_plot <- function(fits) {
  dat <- do.call(rbind, Map(path_data, fits, names(fits)))
  ggplot(dat, aes(lambda, estimate, colour=variable, group=variable)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept=0, colour='grey80') + geom_line(linewidth=0.6) +
    scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method, ncol=2) +
    labs(x=expression(lambda), y=expression(hat(beta)[j]), colour='Variable') +
    theme(legend.position='bottom', legend.box='vertical') +
    guides(colour=guide_legend(nrow=2, byrow=TRUE, order=1))
}
get_diagnostics <- function(fits) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
    d <- dof(fits[[m]])
    data.frame(method=m, lambda=d$lambda, df=d$df,
               status=d$status, nzero=fits[[m]]$nzero)
  }))
}
diagnostics <- get_diagnostics(fits)
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(diagnostics$method, diagnostics$status)),
             col.names=c('Method','Derivative status','Grid points'))
stopifnot(all(diagnostics$status == 'ok'))
knitr::kable(data.frame(method=names(fits),
  nonzero_at_largest_lambda=vapply(fits, function(f) f$nzero[which.max(f$lambda)], numeric(1))), row.names=FALSE)
```

The checks below deliberately stop if a candidate fails the derivative
diagnostics. In an analysis, inspect the reported status before adjusting
solver tolerances or excluding a candidate; do not silently replace missing
DoF by the active-set size.

### Coefficient paths

```{r scalar-paths, fig.cap="Coefficient paths for Lasso and Adaptive Lasso. Colours identify the same variables in both panels; the intercept is omitted."}
coefficient_plot(fits)
```

At the right-hand end, the penalized coefficients are zero. Moving left relaxes
the penalty and allows signal variables, and eventually noise variables, into
the model. Compare how quickly the large signal coefficients approach their
true values under adaptive weighting. Their values at specific knots are
shown next, so that the comparison is not based on visual impressions alone.

```{r slices}
coefficient_slices <- function(fits, indices=c(1, 25, 45, 60)) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
    f <- fits[[m]]
    b <- coef(f, s=f$lambda[indices])
    z <- data.frame(variable=rownames(b), truth=c(intercept_true, beta_true), b,
                    check.names=FALSE)
    names(z)[-(1:2)] <- paste0('lambda=', format(signif(f$lambda[indices],3), trim=TRUE))
    cbind(method=m, z)
  }))
}
knitr::kable(coefficient_slices(fits), digits=3, row.names=FALSE)
```

### Degrees of freedom along the same paths

With an intercept and a full-column-rank design, the fixed-weight Lasso
reference is $1+|A|$: the intercept contributes one degree of freedom.
For Adaptive Lasso the total also includes derivatives of the pilot-based
weights. We compare each method with its **own** active set.

```{r scalar-dof, fig.cap="Divergence and active-coordinate count, including one unpenalized intercept. Points are computed grid values; connecting lines are visual guides."}
plot_dof <- function(d) {
  z <- rbind(data.frame(d, quantity='Divergence', value=d$df),
             data.frame(d, quantity='1 + nonzero coefficients', value=1+d$nzero))
  ggplot(z, aes(lambda, value, colour=quantity, linetype=quantity)) +
    geom_line(linewidth=0.7) + geom_point(size=0.7) + scale_x_log10() +
    facet_wrap(~method, ncol=2) +
    labs(x=expression(lambda), y='Complexity', colour=NULL, linetype=NULL) +
    theme(legend.position='bottom')
}
plot_dof(diagnostics)
```

```{r scalar-dof-summary}
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(split(diagnostics, diagnostics$method), function(d) {
 data.frame(method=d$method[1], min_correction=min(d$df-1-d$nzero),
            max_correction=max(d$df-1-d$nzero))
})), digits=4, row.names=FALSE)
```

The table quantifies departure from the counting rule on this realization.
For the correlated design used here, we do not assume that the adaptive
correction must be positive at every response or every regularization value.
The curve is a response-specific divergence path, not the population DoF
function itself.

## Group Lasso and Adaptive Group Lasso

We now use the known disjoint groups. The data, intercept and regularization
grid stay the same. Group Lasso promotes entire groups entering or leaving
the model; it does not generally create sparsity within an active group.

```{r group-fits}
fit_glasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='glasso', groups=groups,
                    intercept=TRUE, standardize=FALSE,
                    lambda=lambda, control=control)
fit_adaglasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='adaglasso', groups=groups,
                       profile='exponential', exponent=1,
                       intercept=TRUE, standardize=FALSE,
                       lambda=lambda, control=control)
group_fits <- list('Group Lasso'=fit_glasso, 'Adaptive Group Lasso'=fit_adaglasso)
group_diagnostics <- get_diagnostics(group_fits)
stopifnot(all(group_diagnostics$status == 'ok'))
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(group_diagnostics$method, group_diagnostics$status)),
             col.names=c('Method','Derivative status','Grid points'))
```

### Coordinate estimates and group norms

```{r group-paths, fig.cap="Individual coefficient estimates along the group-penalized paths. These are coefficients, not group norms."}
coefficient_plot(group_fits)
```

```{r group-norms, fig.cap="Estimated group norms along the path. The dashed horizontal levels are the true group norms; colours identify groups consistently."}
group_path <- function(fit, method) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(groups), function(g) {
    data.frame(method=method, lambda=fit$lambda, group=factor(g),
               norm=sqrt(colSums(fit$beta[groups==g,,drop=FALSE]^2)),
               truth=sqrt(sum(beta_true[groups==g]^2)))
  }))
}
gp <- do.call(rbind, Map(group_path, group_fits, names(group_fits)))
truths <- unique(gp[c('method','group','truth')])
ggplot(gp, aes(lambda, norm, colour=group)) + geom_line(linewidth=0.7) +
  geom_hline(data=truths, aes(yintercept=truth, colour=group), linetype=3) +
  scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method, ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda), y=expression(group~norm~~rho[g]), colour='Group') +
  theme(legend.position='bottom')
```

The true norm is zero for groups 3 and 4. Their fitted norms show when weak
regularization admits groups containing only noise. Group 2 contains a truly
zero coordinate, but its group is informative: selecting this group does not
imply that all three of its coefficients are truly nonzero.

```{r group-slices}
knitr::kable(coefficient_slices(group_fits), digits=3, row.names=FALSE)
```

### Group counts, dimensions and divergence

```{r group-dof, fig.cap="Total divergence, number of nonzero coordinates, active-group count and active-group dimension. Each count includes the intercept contribution."}
group_counts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(group_fits), function(m) {
  f <- group_fits[[m]]; d <- dof(f)
  active <- attr(d, 'active_groups')
  ng <- d$active_groups
  dimension <- vapply(active, function(a) sum(table(groups)[a]), numeric(1))
  rbind(data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='Divergence',value=d$df),
        data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='1 + nonzero coefficients',value=1+f$nzero),
        data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='1 + active groups',value=1+ng),
        data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='1 + active-group dimension',value=1+dimension))
}))
ggplot(group_counts, aes(lambda,value,colour=quantity,linetype=quantity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=0.7) + scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method,ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda), y='Complexity', colour=NULL,linetype=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position='bottom') +
  guides(colour=guide_legend(nrow=2,byrow=TRUE),
         linetype=guide_legend(nrow=2,byrow=TRUE))
```

Counts use the active groups returned by `dof()`, whose diagnostics distinguish
constrained-zero groups from small numerical residuals. Testing raw fitted
coefficients for exact equality to zero can give misleading counts.

For fixed positive group weights, the penalized divergence lies between the
number of active groups and their total dimension; the plotted totals add
the intercept. The active-group dimension counts **all** coordinates in active
groups, including any individually zero coefficients. The two coordinate-count
curves may overlap in this example. Adaptive weight derivatives introduce
another term, so the fixed-weight bounds should not be transferred unchanged
to the adaptive total.

### Decompose the adaptive divergence

```{r decomposition, fig.cap="Decomposition at the adaptive solutions: total divergence equals the fixed-weight contribution plus the adaptive correction."}
all_fits <- c(fits, group_fits)
adaptive_fits <- all_fits[c('Adaptive Lasso','Adaptive Group Lasso')]
components <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(adaptive_fits), function(m) {
 d <- dof(adaptive_fits[[m]])
 rbind(data.frame(method=m,lambda=d$lambda,component='Total',value=d$df),
       data.frame(method=m,lambda=d$lambda,component='Fixed-weight contribution',value=d$df_fixed),
       data.frame(method=m,lambda=d$lambda,component='Adaptive correction',value=d$adaptive_correction))
}))
ggplot(components,aes(lambda,value,colour=component,linetype=component)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0,colour='grey80') + geom_line(linewidth=0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method,ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda),y='Divergence contribution',colour=NULL,linetype=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position='bottom')
```

The fixed-weight contribution is computed at the **same adaptive solution**,
with the observed weights held constant only during differentiation. It is
not the DoF of the separately fitted ordinary Lasso or Group Lasso.
The correction excludes the intercept contribution, which is already included
in the fixed-weight term.

## Select a location on each path

For each method, we compute effective-DoF BIC, known-variance SURE, and
five-fold CV with a common fold assignment and an explicit common grid.
The adaptive pilot is recomputed in every training fold. Using the true
variance in SURE is possible here because this is a simulation.

```{r selection}
set.seed(2027)
foldid <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out=n))
penalties <- c('lasso','adalasso','glasso','adaglasso')
selected <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(all_fits), function(i) {
 m <- names(all_fits)[i]; f <- all_fits[[i]]
 bic <- select(f, criterion='BIC')
 sure <- select(f, criterion='SURE', sigma2=sigma^2)
 args <- list(X=X,y=y,penalty=penalties[i],intercept=TRUE,
              standardize=FALSE,lambda=lambda,foldid=foldid,control=control)
 if(i>=3) args$groups <- groups
 if(i %in% c(2,4)) {args$profile <- 'exponential'; args$exponent <- 1}
 cv <- do.call(cv.lmreg,args)
 data.frame(method=m,rule=c('BIC','SURE','CV minimum','CV one SE'),
            lambda=c(bic$lambda,sure$lambda,cv$lambda.min,cv$lambda.1se))
}))
knitr::kable(selected,digits=5,row.names=FALSE)
```

### Locate the selected models on both paths

```{r selected-coefficients, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Coefficient paths with vertical lines at each selected regularization value. Coincident choices produce overlapping lines."}
coefficient_plot(all_fits) +
  geom_vline(data=selected,aes(xintercept=lambda,linetype=rule),
             colour='grey25',linewidth=0.55) +
  labs(linetype='Selection rule') +
  guides(linetype=guide_legend(nrow=1,order=2)) +
  theme(legend.box='vertical')
```

```{r selected-dof, fig.height=6, fig.cap="The same tuning choices located on the divergence paths. These are fixed-lambda divergences evaluated at selected knots, not DoF estimates for the entire selection procedure."}
dall <- get_diagnostics(all_fits)
ggplot(dall,aes(lambda,df)) + geom_line(colour='#b5121b',linewidth=0.8) +
  geom_vline(data=selected,aes(xintercept=lambda,linetype=rule),colour='grey30') +
  scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method,ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda),y='Divergence',linetype='Selection rule') +
  theme(legend.position='bottom')
```

BIC, SURE and CV target different criteria and need not select the same knot.
The one-SE choice favours a larger penalty than the CV minimum according to
the reported fold-dispersion rule. It is not an exact uncertainty statement
accounting for overlapping training sets. The fixed-$\lambda$ unbiasedness
result does not automatically apply to the full data-dependent selection rule.

### Evaluate on independent test observations

```{r test-data}
set.seed(2028)
ntest <- 2000
Xtest <- matrix(rnorm(ntest*p),ntest,p) %*% chol(Sigma)
mutest <- as.numeric(intercept_true + Xtest %*% beta_true)
ytest <- mutest + rnorm(ntest,sd=sigma)
performance <- do.call(rbind,lapply(seq_len(nrow(selected)),function(i) {
 s <- selected[i,]; f <- all_fits[[s$method]]
 pred <- as.numeric(predict(f,newx=Xtest,s=s$lambda))
 k <- which.min(abs(f$lambda-s$lambda))
 data.frame(s,nonzero=f$nzero[k],df=dof(f)$df[k],
            mean_MSE=mean((pred-mutest)^2),prediction_MSE=mean((pred-ytest)^2))
}))
knitr::kable(performance,digits=4,row.names=FALSE)
```

`mean_MSE` compares predictions with the known noiseless mean; `prediction_MSE`
compares with new noisy responses and includes irreducible noise. SURE here
targets in-sample fixed-design mean estimation risk, so it need not minimize
this independent random-design test error. The test set is used only after
selection and never determines the chosen regularization value.

```{r interpretation, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
for(m in names(all_fits)) {
 z <- performance[performance$method==m,]
 cat(sprintf('* **%s:** the selected penalties range from %.4f to %.4f, with %d to %d nonzero coefficients. Independent test mean MSE ranges from %.4f to %.4f.\n',
 m,min(z$lambda),max(z$lambda),min(z$nonzero),max(z$nonzero),min(z$mean_MSE),max(z$mean_MSE)))
}
```

These summaries describe this dataset, not a universal advantage of one
method or criterion. Repeated simulations would be needed to assess stability.

## Check the analytic divergence numerically

Stein's expectation identity requires regularity and integrability
[@stein1981sure]. Relevant degrees-of-freedom results include those
for the Lasso [@zou2007] and partly smooth regularizers
[@vaiter_etal.2017]. The finite-difference calculation below checks a
local Jacobian formula; it does not prove those global hypotheses.

For one fixed Adaptive Group Lasso knot, approximate
$\sum_i\partial\widehat\mu_i/\partial y_i$ by centered response perturbations.
We refit the adaptive model for every perturbation, including recomputation
of its pilot and weights. Holding the weights fixed would check a different
Jacobian. The design, regularization value and preprocessing are held fixed.

```{r finite-differences}
f <- fit_adaglasso
k <- which.min(abs(f$lambda-0.1))
lambda_check <- f$lambda[k]
refit_mean <- function(response) {
 fit <- lmreg(X,response,penalty='adaglasso',groups=groups,
              profile='exponential',exponent=1,intercept=TRUE,
              standardize=FALSE,lambda=lambda_check,control=control)
 stopifnot(all(as.numeric(fit$convergence)==1))
 as.numeric(predict(fit,newx=X))
}
finite_difference <- function(h) {
 sum(vapply(seq_len(n),function(i) {
   yp <- ym <- y; yp[i] <- yp[i]+h; ym[i] <- ym[i]-h
   (refit_mean(yp)[i]-refit_mean(ym)[i])/(2*h)
 },numeric(1)))
}
h <- c(1e-3,3e-4)
analytic <- dof(f)$df[k]
fd <- vapply(h,finite_difference,numeric(1))
validation <- data.frame(lambda=lambda_check,step=h,analytic=analytic,
                         numerical=fd,absolute_error=abs(fd-analytic))
validation_display <- validation
validation_display$absolute_error <- formatC(validation$absolute_error, format='e', digits=2)
knitr::kable(validation_display,digits=7,row.names=FALSE)
stopifnot(all(validation$absolute_error < 0.01))
```

Agreement at two step sizes is a local numerical check. Finite differences
can be unreliable at transitions or if solver error dominates the perturbation.
This calculation does not prove weak differentiability or integrability and
therefore does not by itself establish Stein unbiasedness.

## Reproduce and extend the analysis

For prediction-error estimation and the distinction between fitting
and model search, see @efron2004covariance and @tibshirani2015ss.

Every figure and table above is generated by the displayed R code. Change the
seed, correlation, signal strengths or group structure to explore other cases.
For method comparisons, keep the same training/test data and CV folds; do not
select a favourable seed after seeing the results.

For overlapping and sparse-group penalties, the fitting interface is similar,
but the penalty geometry and the scope of the DoF guarantees must be discussed
separately. This tutorial concentrates on the four methods for which the
fixed-weight/adaptive comparison is most direct.

sessionInfo()
```
